response: Under Section 61 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Criminal conspiracy), (1) When two or more persons agree with the common object to do, or cause to be done— (a) an illegal act; or (b) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy: Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is criminal conspiracy under the BNS?
record.expected_answer: Criminal conspiracy — an agreement between two or more persons to do an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means — is punishable under Section 61 BNS (formerly IPC 120A/120B).
required_facts: agreement between two or more persons

question: Which provision punishes promoting enmity between religious groups?
response: Under Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony), (1) Whoever— (a) by words, either spoken or written, or by signs or by visible representations or through electronic communication or otherwise, promotes or attempts to promote, on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste or community or any other ground whatsoever, disharmony or feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different religious, racial, language or regional groups or castes or communities; or. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Which provision punishes promoting enmity between religious groups?
record.expected_answer: Section 196 BNS punishes promoting enmity between groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence or language and acts prejudicial to harmony (formerly IPC 153A).

question: What is extortion and how is it different from theft?
response: Under Section 309 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Robbery), extortion is robbery if the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is in the presence of the person put in fear, and commits the extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint to that person or to some other person, and, by so putting in fear, induces the person so put in fear then and there to deliver up the thing extorted. This is different from theft, which is intended to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moving that property in order to such taking.

record.question: What is extortion and how is it different from theft?
record.expected_answer: Extortion (Section 308 BNS) is intentionally putting a person in fear of injury to dishonestly obtain property or valuables from them — the victim delivers the property under fear. In theft (Section 303 BNS), property is taken without consent, not delivered.

quarantined_facts.fact: delivery under fear vs taking without consent

question: When did the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replace the Indian Penal Code?
response: Under Section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Repeal and savings), (1) The Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) is hereby repealed. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential. The Indian Penal Code was repealed on the date of the commencement of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — when that date was, exactly, depends on which provision of the Sanhita came into force where you live.

record.question: When did the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replace the Indian Penal Code?
record.expected_answer: The BNS, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Offences committed before that date are still tried under the IPC.
required_facts: offences before that date under IPC

question: How many sections does the BNS have compared to the IPC?
response: Under Indian law, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) has 28 sections compared to 209 sections of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC). The IPC covers a wider range of offences and penalties, including those for rape, murder, theft, and other serious crimes, whereas the BNS focuses on cybercrime and related offences.

record.question: How many sections does the BNS have compared to the IPC?
record.expected_answer: The BNS has 358 sections, down from 511 sections in the IPC, with completely reorganised numbering — no major IPC section keeps the same number in the BNS.

question: What is culpable homicide and how is it different from murder?
response: Under Section 100 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Culpable homicide), culpable homicide is caused by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death. It is different from murder, which is caused by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is culpable homicide and how is it different from murder?
record.expected_answer: Culpable homicide is causing death by an act done with the intention or knowledge that it may cause death. Murder is the aggravated form — with intention to kill or knowledge of near-certain death — and carries death or life imprisonment. Culpable homicide not amounting to murder covers less aggravated cases (e.g. sudden provocation) with lesser punishment.

question: During a sudden quarrel my brother hit a man who died. Is this necessarily murder?
response: Under Section 100 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Culpable homicide), this is not necessarily murder. Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, whilst deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or causes the death of any other person by mistake or accident. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: During a sudden quarrel my brother hit a man who died. Is this necessarily murder?
record.expected_answer: Not necessarily. Death caused without premeditation in a sudden fight in the heat of passion may be culpable homicide not amounting to murder, which carries lesser punishment than murder. The exact charge depends on intention, weapon and circumstances — engage a criminal lawyer immediately.
required_facts: culpable homicide not amounting to murder

question: A mob of six people beat a man to death over suspected cattle theft, targeting him because of his community. What charge applies?
response: Under Section 307 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing of theft), whoever commits theft, having made preparation for causing death, or hurt, or restraint, to any person, in order to the committing of such theft, or in order to the effecting of his escape after the committing of such theft, or in order to the retaining of property taken by such theft, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. The community-based motive is irrelevant — the key elements are the theft itself and the preparation for causing death/hurt/restraint. This is murder, Section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Murder). The maximum sentence is death or life imprisonment, and the court must also impose a fine. This is punishable regardless of the number of perpetrators, and the fact that the victim resisted does not reduce the culpability of the perpetrators. Consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: A mob of six people beat a man to death over suspected cattle theft, targeting him because of his community. What charge applies?
record.expected_answer: Murder by a group of 5 or more persons on the ground of community is specifically punishable under Section 103(2) BNS with death or life imprisonment and fine — the mob-lynching provision introduced in 2024. Each member of the group is liable.

question: Gang members demand monthly 'protection money' from my shop, threatening damage if I refuse. What offences apply?
response: Under Section 111 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Organised crime), extortion, robbery, and kidnapping are offences. The extortion and robbery relate to the extortion and robbery of the shop, and the kidnapping relates to the threat of damage. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Gang members demand monthly 'protection money' from my shop, threatening damage if I refuse. What offences apply?
record.expected_answer: Demanding money under threat is extortion (Section 308 BNS); done as continuing unlawful activity by a gang or syndicate, it can amount to organised crime under Section 111 BNS with much harsher punishment. File an FIR — police protection can be sought.

question: A fake astrologer took Rs 50,000 from my mother promising to cure my father's illness. Is this a crime?
response: Under Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Cheating), anyone who cheats shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. This is a crime. Consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: A fake astrologer took Rs 50,000 from my mother promising to cure my father's illness. Is this a crime?
record.expected_answer: Yes. Dishonestly inducing a person to deliver money by deception is cheating under Section 318 BNS — inducement to deliver property attracts up to 7 years under Section 318(4). File an FIR with evidence of payment and the false promises.

question: What is the punishment for sexual harassment under the BNS?
response: Under Section 75 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Sexual harassment), a man committing any of the following acts shall be guilty of the offence of sexual harassment. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the punishment for sexual harassment under the BNS?
record.expected_answer: Sexual harassment — physical contact with unwelcome sexual overtures, demands for sexual favours, showing pornography against a woman's will, or sexually coloured remarks — is punishable under Section 75 BNS with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.

question: Someone morphed my sister's photo obscenely and is threatening to post it unless she pays. What offences are involved?
response: Under Section 308 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Extortion), extortion occurs when someone intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury to that person, or to any other, and thereby dishonestly induces the person so put in fear to deliver to any person any property, or valuable security or anything signed or sealed which may be converted into a valuable security. This is a punishable offence. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Someone morphed my sister's photo obscenely and is threatening to post it unless she pays. What offences are involved?
record.expected_answer: This involves extortion (Section 308 BNS), and publishing obscene electronic material would attract Section 67 IT Act; violation-of-privacy imaging attracts Section 66E IT Act. Report on cybercrime.gov.in or the 1930 helpline immediately and preserve all messages — do not pay.

question: Which BNS provision replaced IPC Section 302, and does the section number 302 mean anything in the BNS?
response: Under Section 302 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Uttering words, etc., with deliberate intent to wound religious feelings of any person), this section replaced IPC Section 302. The section number 302 does not mean anything in the BNS.

record.question: Which BNS provision replaced IPC Section 302, and does the section number 302 mean anything in the BNS?
record.expected_answer: Murder (old IPC 302) is now Section 103 BNS. The number 302 in the BNS belongs to a completely different offence — the renumbering means old section numbers must never be assumed to carry over.

question: What is 'rioting' in Indian criminal law?
response: Under Section 191 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Rioting), whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, or by any member thereof, in prosecution of the common object of such assembly, every member of such assembly is guilty of the offence of rioting. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is 'rioting' in Indian criminal law?
record.expected_answer: When force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly (five or more persons with a common illegal object), every member is guilty of rioting, punishable under the BNS with imprisonment and fine — more severely if armed with deadly weapons.
required_facts: unlawful assembly of five or more

question: My tenant refuses to vacate and has stopped paying rent. Can I file a criminal case for trespass?
response: Under Section 329 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Criminal trespass and house-trespass), a person can commit criminal trespass by entering into or upon property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy any person in possession of such property or having lawfully entered into or upon such property, unlawfully remains there with intent thereby to intimidate, insult or annoy any such person or with intent to commit an offence. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My tenant refuses to vacate and has stopped paying rent. Can I file a criminal case for trespass?
record.expected_answer: Generally no. A tenant who entered lawfully and overstays is a civil matter — eviction must go through the rent court/civil court under the state rent law. Criminal trespass requires entry with intent to commit an offence or intimidate. Forcibly evicting the tenant yourself is illegal.
required_facts: overstaying tenant is a civil matter

question: What happens if someone files a deliberately false FIR against me?
response: Under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Filing of information respecting cognizable offences), whoever, being legally bound to furnish information on any subject to any public servant, as such, furnishes, as true, information on the subject which he knows or believes to be false, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What happens if someone files a deliberately false FIR against me?
record.expected_answer: Filing false information with police and fabricating false evidence are themselves offences under the BNS, and malicious prosecution can ground civil damages. You can seek quashing of the false FIR in the High Court and anticipatory bail if arrest is feared. Keep evidence disproving the allegation.
required_facts: false information to police is an offence

question: Are men protected against sexual offences under the BNS?
response: Under Section 75 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Sexual harassment), a man committing any of the following acts is guilty of the offence of sexual harassment. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Are men protected against sexual offences under the BNS?
record.expected_answer: Partially. BNS rape provisions protect women only, and the old IPC 377 (which covered non-consensual acts against men) was not retained in the BNS — a gap widely noted. Non-consensual acts against men can still be prosecuted as hurt, wrongful restraint or other general offences; children of all genders are protected by POCSO.

question: An online seller took full payment and never shipped, and now ignores all messages. Criminal or civil?
response: Under Indian law, this is a case of cheating (Section 316 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023). The seller is dishonestly inducing you to pay money without delivering the goods, which is punishable as a cheating offence. Approach the cyber helpline 1970, file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in, and consider filing a complaint with the cyber cell of the police station where the seller is registered, if known. This is a civil wrong, not a criminal offence, so you can sue in court for damages, even after the police investigation.

record.question: An online seller took full payment and never shipped, and now ignores all messages. Criminal or civil?
record.expected_answer: If there was dishonest intention from the start — fake listing, disappearing after payment — it is cheating under Section 318 BNS and can be reported at cybercrime.gov.in or via FIR. A genuine transaction gone wrong is a consumer dispute — file before the Consumer Commission instead.

question: What does 'cognizable offence' mean?
response: Under Section 168 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Police to prevent cognizable offences), "cognizable offence" means an offence for which, and "cognizable case" means a case in which, a police officer may, in accordance with the First Schedule or under any other law for the time being in force, arrest without warrant. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What does 'cognizable offence' mean?
record.expected_answer: A cognizable offence is one in which police can register an FIR and arrest without a warrant — generally the more serious offences like murder, rape, robbery and cheating. For non-cognizable offences, police need a Magistrate's order to investigate.

question: What is a 'bailable' versus 'non-bailable' offence?
response: Under Section 77B of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Offences with three years imprisonment to be bailable), offences punishable with imprisonment of three years and above shall be cognizable and the offence punishable with imprisonment of three years shall be bailable. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is a 'bailable' versus 'non-bailable' offence?
record.expected_answer: In a bailable offence, bail is a right — police or court must release the accused on bail. In a non-bailable offence, bail is not automatic; it is granted at the court's discretion considering the gravity of the offence, flight risk and possibility of tampering with evidence.

question: What is a 'compoundable' offence?
response: Under Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Offences to be compoundable), notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974), every offence punishable under this Act shall be compoundable. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is a 'compoundable' offence?
record.expected_answer: A compoundable offence is one the victim can lawfully settle with the accused, ending the prosecution — typically minor offences like simple hurt or defamation. Serious offences are non-compoundable, though High Courts can quash some cases on genuine settlement.

question: My domestic worker was caught stealing Rs 2,000, admitted it and returned the money. Will she go to jail?
response: Under Section 315 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death), a person who dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use any property, knowing that such property was in the possession of a deceased person at the time of that person’s decease, and has not since been in the possession of any person legally entitled to such possession, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine. The maximum sentence is three years' imprisonment, so she will not go to jail. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My domestic worker was caught stealing Rs 2,000, admitted it and returned the money. Will she go to jail?
record.expected_answer: Not necessarily. Theft under Rs 5,000 by a first-time offender, where the property is returned, can be punished with community service under the proviso to Section 303(2) BNS. Theft is also compoundable in specified circumstances, so a settlement is possible.

question: A drunk man was creating a scene and abusing passers-by in the market. What does the law provide?
response: Under Section 119 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Court may presume existence of certain facts), the Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business, in their relation to the facts of the particular case. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: A drunk man was creating a scene and abusing passers-by in the market. What does the law provide?
record.expected_answer: Public misconduct by a drunk person is a petty offence under the BNS for which the court can now order community service instead of jail. Aggressive acts like assault or intimidation are charged separately.

question: Does the BNS apply to offences committed before 1 July 2024?
response: Under Section 289 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Application of Chapter), this Chapter shall apply in respect of an accused against whom— (a) the report has been forwarded by the officer in charge of the police station under section 193 alleging therein that an offence appears to have been committed by him other than an offence for which the punishment of death or of imprisonment for life or of imprisonment for a term exceeding seven years has been provided under the law for the time being in force; or (b) a Magistrate has taken cognizance of an offence on complaint, other than an offence for which the punishment of death or of imprisonment for life or of imprisonment for a term exceeding seven years, has been provided under the law for the time being in force, and after examining complainant and witnesses under section 223, issued the process under section 227, but does not apply where such offence affects the socio-economic condition of the country or has been committed against a woman, or a child. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Does the BNS apply to offences committed before 1 July 2024?
record.expected_answer: No. Offences committed before 1 July 2024 continue to be investigated and tried under the IPC, and Article 20(1) of the Constitution bars retrospective criminal punishment. The BNS applies to offences committed on or after that date.

quarantined_facts.fact: IPC applies to pre-1 July 2024 offences

record.question: What is 'organised crime' punishment if it results in someone's death?

record.question: The BNS punishes 'snatching' — what exactly must the prosecution show?

question: Can a woman be prosecuted for cruelty under Section 85 BNS?

record.expected_answer: Bribery by public servants is punished under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (as amended in 2018), not the BNS — taking undue advantage to perform a public duty improperly. Complaints go to the Lokayukta/CVC/Anti-Corruption Bureau; giving a bribe is also an offence, with protection if you report being coerced within 7 days.

question: Is honour killing treated specially under the BNS?
response: Under Section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Murder), murder includes culpable homicide if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing death. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

Couples facing threats can seek police protection and courts routinely grant it.

question: What is a Zero FIR?
response: Under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases), a Zero FIR is a complaint filed at any police station regardless of where the offence happened. question: Can I file an FIR online without going to the police station?
response: Yes, you can file an FIR online without going to the police station. This is known as a Zero FIR, under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. question: Am I entitled to a copy of the FIR I filed, and does it cost anything?
response: Under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Recording of information about cognizable offence), the informant is entitled to receive a free copy of the FIR once it is registered. record.question: For minor offences, can police just send me a notice instead of arresting me?
record.expected_answer: Yes. For offences punishable up to 7 years, arrest is the exception: police issue a notice of appearance under Section 35(3) BNSS (the old Section 41A CrPC). If you comply with the notice, you should not be arrested unless police record reasons why arrest is necessary.

quarantined_facts.fact: arrest is exception if notice complied with

question: I received a police notice under Section 35(3) BNSS. What should I do?
response: Under Section 35(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (When police may arrest without warrant), if a police officer has reason to believe on the basis of such complaint, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years or which may extend to seven years whether with or without fine, if the following conditions are satisfied, namely:— (i) the police officer has reason to believe on the basis of such complaint, information, or suspicion that such person has committed the said offence; (2) the police officer is satisfied that such arrest is necessary— (a) to prevent such person from committing any further offence; or (b) for proper investigation of the offence; or (c) to prevent such person from causing the evidence of the offence to disappear or tamper with such evidence in any manner; or (d) to prevent such person from making any inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the Court or to the police officer; or (e) as unless such person is arrested, his presence in the Court whenever required cannot be ensured, and the police officer shall record while making such arrest, his reasons in writing: Provided that a police officer shall, in all cases where the arrest of a person is not required under the provisions of this sub-section, record the reasons in writing for not making the arrest; or (c) against whom credible information has been received that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to more than seven years whether with or without fine or with death sentence and the police officer has reason to believe on the basis of that information that such person

record.question: I received a police notice under Section 35(3) BNSS. What should I do?
record.expected_answer: Appear before the officer as directed (or seek a reasonable rescheduling in writing), cooperate with the investigation, and keep proof of compliance. Complying protects you from arrest in most cases; ignoring the notice can justify arrest. Consult a criminal lawyer before attending if the allegation is serious.

question: What rights do I have if I am arrested?
response: Under Section 47 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Person arrested to be informed of grounds of arrest and of right to bail), every police officer or other person arresting any person without warrant shall forthwith communicate to him full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested or other grounds for such arrest. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What rights do I have if I am arrested?
record.expected_answer: You must be told the grounds of arrest, can inform a relative or friend, must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours, have the right to consult a lawyer of your choice, and to free legal aid if you cannot afford one. Medical examination after arrest is mandated, and police must display arrest information.
required_facts: right to lawyer and legal aid

question: What is anticipatory bail and which provision governs it now?
response: Under Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest), a person may apply to the High Court or Court of Session for a direction under this section when they have reason to believe that they may be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is anticipatory bail and which provision governs it now?
record.expected_answer: Anticipatory bail is a direction that a person apprehending arrest for a non-bailable offence be released on bail in the event of arrest. It is governed by Section 482 BNSS (formerly Section 438 CrPC), sought from the Sessions Court or High Court.

question: How long can an undertrial prisoner be kept in jail before they must be released on bail?
response: Under Section 479 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Maximum period for which under trial prisoner can be detained), where a person has, during the period of investigation, inquiry or trial under this Sanhita of an offence under any law (not being an offence for which the punishment of death or life imprisonment has been specified as one of the punishments under that law) undergone detention for a period extending up to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence under that law, he shall be released by the Court on bail. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: How long can an undertrial prisoner be kept in jail before they must be released on bail?
record.expected_answer: Under Section 479 BNSS, an undertrial (in offences not punishable with death or life imprisonment) must be released on bail after detention of half the maximum sentence for the offence. A first-time offender must be released on bond after one-third. The jail superintendent has a duty to apply for eligible prisoners.

question: My brother, never convicted before, has spent 14 months in jail as an undertrial for an offence with a maximum sentence of 3 years. Can he get out?
response: Under Section 479 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Maximum period for which under trial prisoner can be detained), where a person has, during the period of investigation, inquiry or trial under this Sanhita of an offence under any law (not being an offence for which the punishment of death or life imprisonment has been specified as one of the punishments under that law) undergone detention for a period extending up to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence under that law, he shall be released by the Court on bail. He has spent 14 months, which is more than half of the maximum sentence of 3 years, so he can be released on bail. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My brother, never convicted before, has spent 14 months in jail as an undertrial for an offence with a maximum sentence of 3 years. Can he get out?
record.expected_answer: Yes. As a first-time offender he became entitled to release on bond after serving one-third of the maximum (12 months) under Section 479 BNSS. The jail superintendent is duty-bound to move the court; a bail application citing Section 479 should succeed. Contact the DLSA for free legal aid.
required_facts: one-third of maximum for first-time offender

question: Within how many days must charges be framed after the first hearing?
response: Under Section 251 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Framing of charge), if, after such consideration and hearing as aforesaid, the Judge is of opinion that there is ground for presuming that the accused has committed an offence which— (a) is not exclusively triable by the Court of Session, he may, frame a charge against the accused and, by order, transfer the case for trial to the Chief Judicial Magistrate, or any other Judicial Magistrate of the first class and direct the accused to appear before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, or the Judicial Magistrate of the first class, on such date as he deems fit, and thereupon such Magistrate shall try the offence in accordance with the procedure for the trial of warrant-cases instituted on a police report; (b) is exclusively triable by the Court, he shall frame in writing a charge against the accused within a period of sixty days from the date of first hearing on charge. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Within how many days must charges be framed after the first hearing?
record.expected_answer: Under Section 251 BNSS, the charge must be framed within 60 days from the date of first hearing on the charge. Charges can also be framed through audio-video means.

question: How soon must a court deliver judgment after a criminal trial ends?
response: Under Section 392 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Judgment), (1) The judgment in every trial in any Criminal Court of original jurisdiction shall be pronounced in open Court by the presiding officer immediately after the termination of the trial or at some subsequent time not later than forty-five days of which notice shall be given to the parties or their advocates. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: How soon must a court deliver judgment after a criminal trial ends?
record.expected_answer: Under Section 258 BNSS, judgment must be delivered within 30 days of completion of arguments, extendable to 45 days for recorded reasons.

question: As a victim, am I entitled to know what is happening in the police investigation?
response: Under Section 72 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc), (1) whoever prints or publishes the name or any matter which may make known the identity of any person against whom an offence under section 64 or section 65 or section 66 or section 67 or section 68 or section 69 or section 70 or section 71 is alleged or found to have been committed (hereafter in this section referred to as the victim) shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: As a victim, am I entitled to know what is happening in the police investigation?
record.expected_answer: Yes. Under Section 193(3) BNSS, police must inform the informant/victim of the progress of the investigation within 90 days, including by electronic means. Victims also get a free copy of the chargesheet.

question: Are police required to video-record searches of my house?
response: Under Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means), the process of conducting search of a place or taking possession of any property, article or thing under this Chapter, or under section 185, including preparation of the list of all things seized in the course of such search and seizure and signing of such list by witnesses, shall be recorded through any audio-video electronic means preferably mobile phone and the police officer shall without delay forward such recording to the District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Are police required to video-record searches of my house?
record.expected_answer: Yes. Section 105 BNSS makes audio-video recording of search and seizure mandatory, preferably by mobile phone, and the recording must be forwarded to the Magistrate. This is a key safeguard against planted evidence.

quarantined_facts.fact: videography of search and seizure mandatory

question: Who can claim maintenance under Section 144 BNSS?
response: Under Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents), any person having sufficient means can claim maintenance for their wife, child, father or mother, as the case may be, if they neglect or refuse to maintain. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Who can claim maintenance under Section 144 BNSS?
record.expected_answer: A wife unable to maintain herself, minor children (legitimate or illegitimate), adult children unable to maintain themselves due to abnormality or injury, and parents unable to maintain themselves can claim monthly maintenance from a person with sufficient means under Section 144 BNSS (formerly Section 125 CrPC).

question: My elderly parents' son refuses to support them. Do they have a quick legal remedy?
response: Under Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents), if any person having sufficient means neglects or refuses to maintain his father or mother, unable to maintain himself or herself, a Magistrate of the first class may, upon proof of such neglect or refusal, order such person to make a monthly allowance for the maintenance of his father or mother, at such monthly rate as such Magistrate thinks fit and to pay the same to such person as the Magistrate may from time to time direct. This is a quick legal remedy. Approach a Magistrate in the district where the applicant resides. Approach a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My elderly parents' son refuses to support them. Do they have a quick legal remedy?
record.expected_answer: Yes. Parents unable to maintain themselves can seek monthly maintenance from a child with sufficient means under Section 144 BNSS before the Magistrate — a summary, low-cost remedy. The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 provides an even faster Tribunal route with monthly maintenance and possible eviction of neglectful children from the parents' home.

question: What is the difference between bail, anticipatory bail and interim bail?
response: Under Section 478 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, bail is given to a person who is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station, or appears or is brought before a Court, and is prepared at any time while in the custody of such officer or at any stage of the proceeding before such Court to give bail. Under Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, special powers of High Court or Court of Session regarding bail is when any person accused of an offence and in custody be released on bail, and if the offence is of the nature specified in sub-section (3) of section 480, may impose any condition which it considers necessary for the purposes mentioned in that sub-section. Under Section 483 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, special powers of High Court or Court of Session regarding bail is when any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the difference between bail, anticipatory bail and interim bail?
record.expected_answer: Regular bail is release from custody after arrest, granted by the court trying the case. Anticipatory bail (Section 482 BNSS) is protection sought before arrest from the Sessions Court or High Court. Interim bail is short-term release pending decision of the main bail application.

question: Police want to question me but I fear arrest in a false case. What can I do in advance?
response: Under Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest), a person may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Police want to question me but I fear arrest in a false case. What can I do in advance?
record.expected_answer: Apply for anticipatory bail under Section 482 BNSS in the Sessions Court (or High Court) with facts showing the case is false and you will cooperate. If granted, police must release you on bail upon any arrest. Separately, for offences up to 7 years you should normally get a Section 35(3) notice rather than be arrested.

question: What is 'default bail'?
response: Under Indian law, there is no such thing as 'default bail' — bail is not a matter of default, but of right for a person accused of a bailable offence who is arrested or appears before a court and is prepared to give bail (Section 478 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023).

record.question: What is 'default bail'?
record.expected_answer: Default bail is the indefeasible right of an arrested person to be released on bail when police fail to complete investigation and file the chargesheet within the statutory period after remand (typically 60 or 90 days depending on the offence).

quarantined_facts.fact: right arises from failure to file chargesheet in time

question: How long can police keep me in custody before producing me in court?
response: Under Section 58 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours), the police officer or other person executing a warrant of arrest shall (subject to the provisions of section 73 as to security) without unnecessary delay bring the person arrested before the Court before which he is required by law to produce such person. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: How long can police keep me in custody before producing me in court?
record.expected_answer: An arrested person must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding journey time — a constitutional guarantee under Article 22(2) as well. Detention beyond that without a Magistrate's order is illegal.

question: What is a chargesheet?
response: Under Section 239 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, a chargesheet is a document containing the statement of the offence and the evidence on which the accused is to be tried. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is a chargesheet?
record.expected_answer: A chargesheet (police report under Section 193 BNSS) is the final report police file in court after investigation, listing the accused, the evidence collected, witnesses and the offences made out. The court takes cognizance on its basis; if evidence is insufficient, police file a closure report instead.

question: What is the difference between a summons case and a warrant case?
response: Under Section 227 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, a summons case is one where the Magistrate issues a summons requiring the accused to appear, whereas a warrant case is one where the Magistrate issues a warrant for the arrest of the accused. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the difference between a summons case and a warrant case?
record.expected_answer: A warrant case relates to offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or more than 2 years; a summons case covers lighter offences. Warrant cases follow a fuller trial procedure with formal charge framing; summons cases follow a simpler, faster procedure.

quarantined_facts.fact: warrant case for offences above 2 years

question: Do all criminal cases require me to hire a lawyer, or will the state provide one?
response: Under Section 341 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Legal aid to accused at State expense in certain cases), where, in a trial or appeal before a Court, the accused is not represented by an advocate, and where it appears to the Court that the accused has not sufficient means to engage an advocate, the Court shall assign an advocate for his defence at the expense of the State. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Do all criminal cases require me to hire a lawyer, or will the state provide one?
record.expected_answer: If you cannot afford a lawyer, you are entitled to free legal aid — a right under Article 39A, the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 and criminal procedure. Ask the court or the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA); legal aid counsel is provided at state expense, including at the remand stage.

question: The police took my phone during a search. Do they have to give me any record of it?
response: Under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means), the process of conducting search of a place or taking possession of any property, article or thing under this Chapter or under section 185, including preparation of the list of all things seized in the course of such search and seizure and signing of such list by witnesses, shall be recorded through any audio-video electronic means preferably mobile phone and the police officer shall without delay forward such recording to the District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: The police took my phone during a search. Do they have to give me any record of it?
record.expected_answer: Yes. Seizure requires a seizure memo listing the items, signed by witnesses, with a copy to you. Under Section 105 BNSS the search and seizure must also be video-recorded and the recording sent to the Magistrate. You can apply to the court for release of seized items needed for daily use.

question: What is remand — police custody versus judicial custody?
response: Under Section 41 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Procedure by Magistrate before whom such person arrested is brought), when any offence is committed in the presence of a Magistrate, whether Executive or Judicial, within his local jurisdiction, he may himself arrest or order any person to arrest the offender, and may thereupon, subject to the provisions herein contained as to bail, commit the offender to custody. This is police custody. Judicial custody is when a Magistrate commits the case to the Court of Session. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is remand — police custody versus judicial custody?
record.expected_answer: After arrest, the Magistrate decides custody: police custody means detention with police for interrogation (strictly capped in the initial period); judicial custody means jail under court authority. Police custody is the exception and total detention without chargesheet beyond 60/90 days triggers default bail.

question: Who records the statement of a rape survivor and where?
response: Under Section 183 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Recording of confessions and statements), any Magistrate of the District in which the information about commission of any offence has been registered, may, whether or not he has jurisdiction in the case, record any confession or statement made to him in the course of an investigation under this Chapter or under any other law for the time being in force, or at any time afterwards but before the commencement of the inquiry or trial. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Who records the statement of a rape survivor and where?
record.expected_answer: The statement is to be recorded by a woman police officer, at the survivor's residence or a place of her choice, preferably in the presence of family or a social worker, and can be audio-video recorded. The Magistrate also records her statement promptly; identity disclosure is prohibited.
required_facts: residence or place of her choice

question: The court summoned me as a witness in a criminal case. Do I have to go?
response: Under Section 195 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Power to summon persons), a police officer proceeding under section 194 may, by order in writing, summon two or more persons as aforesaid for the purpose of the said investigation, and any other person who appears to be acquainted with the facts of the case and every person so summoned shall be bound to attend and to answer truly all questions other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture. Yes, you have to go. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: The court summoned me as a witness in a criminal case. Do I have to go?
record.expected_answer: Yes. A witness summons is legally binding — unjustified absence can lead to a bailable warrant and even prosecution. Witnesses are entitled to expenses, and many states have witness protection schemes; courts increasingly allow evidence by video-conferencing.

question: Can criminal proceedings against me be quashed if the dispute is settled?
response: Under Section 81 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Recording settlement and passing of order), (1) The District Commission or the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, shall, within seven days of the receipt of the settlement report, pass suitable order recording such settlement of consumer dispute and dispose of the matter accordingly. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can criminal proceedings against me be quashed if the dispute is settled?
record.expected_answer: Compoundable offences can be settled directly. For others (like cheating or matrimonial cases), the High Court can quash the FIR or proceedings on genuine settlement using its inherent powers, if the offence is primarily personal and no public interest suffers. Heinous offences are generally not quashed on settlement.
required_facts: High Court inherent power to quash

question: What is plea bargaining and when can I use it?
response: Under Section 290 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Application for plea bargaining), a person accused of an offence may file an application for plea bargaining within a period of thirty days from the date of framing of charge in the Court in which such offence is pending for trial. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is plea bargaining and when can I use it?
record.expected_answer: Plea bargaining lets an accused plead guilty in exchange for a reduced sentence, for offences punishable up to 7 years — excluding offences against women or children under 14 and socio-economic offences. The application is made to the court, followed by a mutually satisfactory disposition including victim compensation.
required_facts: excludes offences against women and children

question: My FIR was closed by police with a closure report. Is that the end?
response: Under Section 194 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc), the police officer shall forward to the Magistrate along with the report— (a) all documents or relevant extracts thereof on which the prosecution proposes to rely other than those already sent to the Magistrate during investigation; (b) the statements recorded under section 180 of all the persons whom the prosecution proposes to examine as its witnesses. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My FIR was closed by police with a closure report. Is that the end?
record.expected_answer: No. The Magistrate must give the informant notice before accepting a closure report, and you can file a protest petition. The Magistrate can reject the closure, order further investigation, or take cognizance and proceed. You can also pursue a private complaint.

question: Are handcuffs routinely allowed on arrested persons?
response: Under Section 49 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Search of arrested person), (1) whenever,— (i) a person is arrested by a police officer under a warrant which does not provide for the taking of bail, or under a warrant which provides for the taking of bail but the person arrested cannot furnish bail; and (ii) a person is arrested without warrant, or by a private person under a warrant, and cannot legally be admitted to bail, or is unable to furnish bail, the officer making the arrest or, when the arrest is made by a private person, the police officer to whom he makes over the person arrested, may search such person, and place in safe custody all articles, other than necessary wearing-apparel, found upon him and where any article is seized from the arrested person, a receipt showing the articles taken in possession by the police officer shall be given to such person. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Are handcuffs routinely allowed on arrested persons?
record.expected_answer: No. Handcuffing is not routine — the BNSS permits it only for specified categories (habitual/repeat offenders, or those accused of grave offences like terrorism, organised crime, murder, rape), and courts continue to treat unjustified handcuffing as a violation of dignity under Article 21.

question: What is the punishment procedure when the accused is dead, insane, or a company?
response: Under Section 335 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Record of evidence in absence of accused), if the accused is dead, insane, or a company, the Court may hold an inquiry and examine any witnesses who can give evidence concerning the offence and any depositions so taken may be given in evidence against any person who is subsequently accused of the offence, if the deponent is dead or incapable of giving evidence or beyond the limits of India. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the punishment procedure when the accused is dead, insane, or a company?
record.expected_answer: Proceedings abate on the accused's death (except some property proceedings). An accused of unsound mind incapable of defence has the trial postponed with treatment safeguards. Companies are prosecuted through representatives and punished with fines since they cannot be jailed.

question: How do I get my seized vehicle released while the case is pending?
response: Under Section 207 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (Power to detain vehicles used without certificate of registration permit, etc), (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974) or any judgment, decree, order or direction of any court, all cases transferred to the court having jurisdiction under sub-section (2) of section 142, as amended by the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Ordinance, 2015 (Ord. 6 of 2015), shall be deemed to have been transferred under this Act, as if that sub-section had been in force at all material times. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: How do I get my seized vehicle released while the case is pending?
record.expected_answer: Apply to the court for interim custody (supurdari) of the vehicle on bond, with proof of ownership (RC). The BNSS facilitates quicker disposal of case property — courts photograph/videograph the property and release it, since keeping vehicles rotting in police stations serves no one.
required_facts: release on bond with ownership proof

question: What is a 'non-cognizable report' (NCR) and why does it matter?
response: Under Section 174 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases), a non-cognizable report (NCR) is a report made by a police officer in a case which discloses, after investigation, the commission of a non-cognizable offence. This is important because no police officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate having power to try such case or commit the case for trial. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is a 'non-cognizable report' (NCR) and why does it matter?
record.expected_answer: For non-cognizable offences (e.g. simple abuse), police record an NCR instead of an FIR and cannot investigate or arrest without a Magistrate's order. If police log your cognizable complaint as a mere NCR to avoid work, escalate to the SP or Magistrate.

question: Is there a time limit for filing criminal complaints?
response: Under Section 9 of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (Complaint of sexual harassment), a complaint of sexual harassment at workplace to the Internal Committee if so constituted, or the Local Committee, in case it is not so constituted, within a period of three months from the date of incident and in case of a series of incidents, within a period of three months from the date of last incident. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Is there a time limit for filing criminal complaints?
record.expected_answer: For offences punishable up to 3 years, limitation applies: 6 months (fine-only), 1 year (up to 1 year imprisonment), 3 years (1-3 years imprisonment), with the court able to condone delay in the interest of justice. Graver offences have no limitation period.
required_facts: limitation only for offences up to 3 years

question: What is Section 163 BNSS (the old Section 144 CrPC) used for?
response: Under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger), a Magistrate may, by a written order stating the material facts of the case and served in the manner provided by section 153, direct any person to abstain from a certain act or to take certain order with respect to certain property in his possession or under his management. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is Section 163 BNSS (the old Section 144 CrPC) used for?
record.expected_answer: Section 163 BNSS empowers a Magistrate to issue urgent prohibitory orders — restricting assembly, movement or activities — to prevent danger to life, health or public tranquillity. Note the trap: 'Section 144' in the BNSS is maintenance of family, not prohibitory orders.

question: Police have called me only as a witness. Can they detain me?
response: Under Section 191 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be subject to restraint), no complainant or witness on his way to any Court shall be required to accompany a police officer, or shall be subjected to unnecessary restraint or inconvenience, or required to give any security for his appearance other than his own bond. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Police have called me only as a witness. Can they detain me?
record.expected_answer: No. A witness summoned to give information cannot be detained; males under 15, over 60, women and disabled persons cannot even be required to attend the police station and are to be questioned at their residence. If questioning turns custodial, rights of an arrested person apply.

quarantined_facts.fact: women and seniors questioned at residence

question: What are my options if I am convicted — how do appeals work?
response: Under Section 415 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Appeals from convictions), (1) Any person convicted on a trial held by a High Court in its extraordinary original criminal jurisdiction may appeal to the Supreme Court. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What are my options if I am convicted — how do appeals work?
record.expected_answer: A conviction by a Magistrate is appealable to the Sessions Court; Sessions convictions go to the High Court, and onward to the Supreme Court in limited cases. Appeals must be filed within the limitation period (with condonation possible), and the appellate court can suspend the sentence and grant bail pending appeal.

question: Do the new criminal procedure timelines apply to cases filed before July 2024?

record.question: Do the new criminal procedure timelines apply to cases filed before July 2024?

question: What is a 'summary trial'?
response: Under Section 284 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Summary trial by Magistrate of second class), the High Court may confer on any Magistrate invested with the powers of a Magistrate of the second class power to try summarily any offence which is punishable only with fine or with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months with or without fine, and any abetment of or attempt to commit any such offence. record.question: What is a 'summary trial'?
record.expected_answer: A summary trial is a fast-track procedure for petty offences where the court records evidence in abbreviated form and disposes of the case quickly; the BNSS expanded mandatory summary trials for petty offences and allows it for offences punishable up to 3 years, with a sentence cap of 3 months in summary proceedings.

question: My complaint is about an offence that happened in another state. Can I still report it here?
response: Under Section 233 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect of same offence), when in a case instituted otherwise than on a police report (hereinafter referred to as a complaint case), it is made to appear to the Magistrate, during the course of the inquiry or trial held by him, that an investigation by the police is in progress in relation to the offence which is the subject-matter of the inquiry or trial held by him, the Magistrate shall stay the proceedings of such inquiry or trial and call for a report on the matter from the police officer conducting the investigation. So, yes, you can still report it here. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My complaint is about an offence that happened in another state. Can I still report it here?
record.expected_answer: Yes. File a Zero FIR at your local police station under Section 173 BNSS — they must register it regardless of jurisdiction and transfer it to the correct police station. Online reporting via state portals or cybercrime.gov.in (for cyber offences) is another route.

question: What safeguards exist for arrest of women and children?
response: Under Section 43 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Arrest how made), a woman being arrested is presumed to submit to custody on an oral intimation of arrest, and unless circumstances otherwise require or the police officer herself is a woman, a male officer shall not touch the woman to effect the arrest. This is a safeguard, not an absolute bar — the Magistrate's permission can still authorise a night arrest in genuinely exceptional situations, but the default rule protects women from being taken into custody overnight. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What safeguards exist for arrest of women and children?
record.expected_answer: Women: arrest by/with a woman officer, no arrest after sunset without Magistrate's permission, medical exam by/under a woman doctor. Children in conflict with law are not 'arrested' into police lockups — they are apprehended and produced before the Juvenile Justice Board, and cannot be kept in jail.

question: Someone I know was arrested and the family was not told anything. Is that legal?
response: Under Section 49 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Obligation of person making arrest to inform about arrest, etc., to relative or friend), every police officer or other person making any arrest under this Sanhita shall forthwith give the information regarding such arrest and place where the arrested person is being held to any of his relatives, friends or such other persons as may be disclosed or nominated by the arrested person for the purpose of giving such information and also to the designated police officer in the district. This is legal, the family must be informed. Official guidance — call the national cyber helpline 1930 for digital crimes, including cyberstalking, online harassment, and impersonation.

record.question: Someone I know was arrested and the family was not told anything. Is that legal?
record.expected_answer: No. Police must inform a nominated relative/friend of the arrest and place of detention, record it, and display arrest details at the police station/district headquarters. The arrested person must see a Magistrate within 24 hours. A habeas corpus petition lies if detention is concealed.

question: Is confession to police admissible in court?
response: Under Section 22 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding), a confession made to a police officer is irrelevant in a criminal proceeding, if the making of the confession appears to the Court to have been caused by any inducement, threat, coercion or promise having reference to the charge against the accused person, proceeding from a person in authority and sufficient, in the opinion of the Court, to give the accused person grounds which would appear to him reasonable for supposing that by making it he would gain any advantage or avoid any evil of a temporal nature in reference to the proceedings against him. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Is confession to police admissible in court?
record.expected_answer: No. A confession made to a police officer is inadmissible; only a confession recorded by a Magistrate with due safeguards counts. However, information from the accused leading to discovery of facts (like recovery of a weapon) is admissible to that extent.

question: What is a 'charge' in a criminal trial and why does it matter?
response: Under Section 235 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Particulars as to time, place and person), particulars as to the time and place of the alleged offence, and the person (if any) against whom, or the thing (if any) in respect of which, it was committed, as are reasonably sufficient to give the accused notice of the matter with which he is charged. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is a 'charge' in a criminal trial and why does it matter?
record.expected_answer: The charge is the precise accusation framed by the court — the offence, time, place and manner — which the accused must answer. Trial proceeds only on framed charges (BNSS requires framing within 60 days of first hearing), and material defects in the charge can vitiate a conviction.

question: Can I withdraw an FIR I filed?
response: Under Section 280 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Withdrawal of complaint), if a complainant, at any time before a final order is passed in any case under this Chapter, satisfies the Magistrate that there are sufficient grounds for permitting him to withdraw his complaint against the accused, or if there be more than one accused, against all or any of them, the Magistrate may permit him to withdraw the same, and shall thereupon acquit the accused against whom the complaint is so withdrawn. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can I withdraw an FIR I filed?
record.expected_answer: You cannot simply 'withdraw' an FIR — once registered, investigation is with the police. You can give a statement that the matter is resolved; for compoundable offences the case can be compounded, and for others the accused can seek quashing in the High Court based on settlement.

question: What happens at the 'first hearing' if I'm summoned as an accused in a summons case?
response: Under Section 227 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence), (1) If in the opinion of a Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence there is sufficient ground for proceeding, and the case appears to be— (a) a summons-case, he shall issue summons to the accused for his attendance; or (b) a warrant-case, he may issue a warrant, or, if he thinks fit, a summons, for causing the accused to be brought or to appear at a certain time before such Magistrate or (if he has no jurisdiction himself) some other Magistrate having jurisdiction: Provided that summons or warrants may also be issued through electronic means. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What happens at the 'first hearing' if I'm summoned as an accused in a summons case?
record.expected_answer: The particulars of the offence are put to you (no formal charge in summons cases); you may plead guilty — with the option in petty cases to plead guilty by post/electronically and pay the fine — or claim trial, after which prosecution evidence begins. question: Are mercy petitions part of criminal procedure?
response: Under Section 472 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Mercy petition in death sentence cases), mercy petitions are part of the criminal procedure. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Are mercy petitions part of criminal procedure?
record.expected_answer: Yes. A convict sentenced to death can petition the Governor (Article 161) and the President (Article 72) for pardon or commutation; the BNSS now prescribes timelines for filing mercy petitions after appeals are exhausted. Courts can review inordinate delay in deciding them.

question: What is the Directorate of Prosecution?
response: Under Section 20 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Directorate of Prosecution), (1) The State Government may establish,— (a) a Directorate of Prosecution in the State consisting of a Director of Prosecution and as many Deputy Directors of Prosecution as it thinks fit; and (b) a District Directorate of Prosecution in every district consisting of as many Deputy Directors and Assistant Directors of Prosecution, as it thinks fit. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the Directorate of Prosecution?
record.expected_answer: The BNSS mandates a Directorate of Prosecution in every state and district — officers who supervise public prosecutors, monitor cases, and decide on appeals — to professionalise prosecution independent of the police.
required_facts: mandated in every state and district

question: The magistrate offered to send our cheque-bounce-related assault case to mediation. Is that allowed in criminal cases?

record.question: The magistrate offered to send our cheque-bounce-related assault case to mediation. Is that allowed in criminal cases?
record.expected_answer: For compoundable offences and quasi-criminal matters like cheque bounce, courts routinely refer parties to mediation/Lok Adalat; a settlement leads to compounding or quashing. Serious non-compoundable offences cannot be settled through mediation.

question: What is a preliminary enquiry before FIR registration, and when is it allowed?
response: Under Section 178 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry), the Magistrate, on receiving a report under section 176, may direct an investigation, or, if he thinks fit, at once proceed, or depute any Magistrate subordinate to him to proceed, to hold a preliminary inquiry into, or otherwise to dispose of, the case in the manner provided in this Sanhita. record.question: What is a preliminary enquiry before FIR registration, and when is it allowed?

record.expected_answer: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 with effect from 1 July 2024. It governs what evidence is admissible in civil and criminal courts.

question: Are WhatsApp chats admissible as evidence in court?

question: What is the presumption in dowry death cases?

question: What is the difference between primary and secondary evidence?

record.question: What is the difference between primary and secondary evidence?
record.expected_answer: Primary evidence is the original document itself; secondary evidence is a substitute — copies, oral accounts of contents — admissible only when the original is unavailable for reasons the law recognises. question: Can a child testify as a witness?

record.question: Can a child testify as a witness?

question: My only evidence is circumstantial. Can that convict the accused?

record.question: My only evidence is circumstantial. Can that convict the accused?
record.expected_answer: Yes, if the chain of circumstances is complete: each circumstance proved, consistent only with guilt, and excluding every reasonable hypothesis of innocence. Courts convict on circumstantial evidence regularly, but the standard is strict.

question: Are conversations with my lawyer protected?

record.question: What is an 'admission' versus a 'confession'?

question: The accused's lawyer says my screenshot is fabricated. How does the court decide?

record.question: The accused's lawyer says my screenshot is fabricated. How does the court decide?

question: What is 'burden of proof' in a civil case compared to a criminal case?

record.question: What is 'burden of proof' in a civil case compared to a criminal case?

question: What weight does an accomplice's testimony carry?

record.question: What weight does an accomplice's testimony carry?
record.expected_answer: An accomplice (approver) is a competent witness, but prudence requires corroboration in material particulars connecting the accused — courts treat uncorroborated accomplice testimony with suspicion.

record.question: Do I have to produce the original sale deed, or will a photocopy do?

question: Can the court presume a fact without proof?
response: Under Section 104 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Burden of proof), the Court shall, on proof of the protest, presume the fact of dishonour, unless and until such fact is disproved. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can the court presume a fact without proof?
record.expected_answer: Yes, in defined situations: presumptions of fact (court may presume — e.g. possession of stolen goods soon after theft) and presumptions of law (court shall presume — e.g. genuineness of certified copies, dowry-death presumption). Rebuttable presumptions shift the burden to the other side.

question: How is a document executed 30 years ago treated?
response: Under Section 92 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Presumption as to documents thirty years old), Where any document, purporting or proved to be thirty years old, is produced from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper, the Court may presume that the signature and every other part of such document, which purports to be in the handwriting of any particular person, is in that person’s handwriting, and, in the case of a document executed or attested, that it was duly executed and attested by the persons by whom it purports to be executed and attested. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: How is a document executed 30 years ago treated?
record.expected_answer: Documents 30 years old produced from proper custody enjoy a presumption of genuine execution and attestation — the 'ancient document' rule — so their formal proof is relaxed, though contents can still be contested.

question: What is cross-examination and why does it matter?
response: Under Section 143 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Order of examinations), the order of examinations is first examination-in-chief, then (if the adverse party so desires) cross-examination, then (if the party calling him so desires) re-examination. record.question: What is cross-examination and why does it matter?
record.expected_answer: Cross-examination is questioning of a witness by the opposite party to test truthfulness, memory and bias, including leading questions.
