question: The eyewitness gave a slightly different account in court than in his police statement. Is his evidence destroyed?
response: Under Indian law, the statement made to the police is not destroyed by the court evidence. Section 181 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — Statements to police and use thereof — (1) No statement made by any person to a police officer in the course of an investigation under this Chapter, shall, if reduced to writing, be signed by the person making it; nor shall any such statement or any record thereof, whether in a police diary or otherwise, or any part of such statement or record, be used for any purpose, save as hereinafter provided, at any inquiry or trial in respect of any offence under investigation at the time when such statement was made: Provided that when any witness is called for the prosecution in such inquiry or trial whose statement has been reduced into writing as aforesaid, any part of his statement, if duly proved, may be used by the accused, and with the permission of the Court, by the prosecution, to contradict such witness in the manner provided by section 148 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023; and when any part of such statement is so used, any part thereof may also be used in the re-examination of such witness, but for the purpose only of explaining any matter referred to in his cross-examination. (2) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to apply to any statement falling within the provisions of clause (a) of section 26 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023; or to affect the provisions of the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 23 of that Adhiniyam. record.question: The eyewitness gave a slightly different account in court than in his police statement. Is his evidence destroyed?
record.expected_answer: Not necessarily. Minor discrepancies are natural and do not discredit a witness; material contradictions on core facts do. The police statement can be used to contradict him, and the court separates the grain from the chaff.

question: Are Google Maps location history or Aadhaar authentication logs usable in court?

record.question: Are Google Maps location history or Aadhaar authentication logs usable in court?
record.expected_answer: Yes — they are electronic records admissible under Section 63 BSA with a proper certificate from the record-keeper, subject to relevancy and privacy safeguards. Courts assess reliability of the underlying system and chain of custody.

question: Does silence of the accused prove guilt?

record.question: Does silence of the accused prove guilt?
record.expected_answer: No. The accused has a constitutional right against self-incrimination (Article 20(3)) and their silence cannot substitute for prosecution proof, though failure to explain incriminating circumstances within their special knowledge can be an additional link in a circumstantial case.

question: What is 'res gestae' or 'part of the same transaction'?
response: Under Section 4 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction), facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue or a relevant fact as to form part of the same transaction, are relevant, whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is 'res gestae' or 'part of the same transaction'?
record.expected_answer: Statements and acts so connected with the incident as to form part of the same transaction — like a spontaneous cry naming the attacker during the assault — are admissible even though otherwise hearsay, because spontaneity leaves no room for fabrication.

question: Is hearsay evidence allowed?

record.question: Is hearsay evidence allowed?
record.expected_answer: Generally no — a witness must depose to what they personally perceived. Exceptions exist: dying declarations (Section 26 BSA), statements in the course of the same transaction, admissions, and statements of persons who cannot be called (dead/unavailable) in defined situations.

question: My accused brother-in-law's phone had photos of the stolen jewellery. What evidentiary principle applies?

This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My accused brother-in-law's phone had photos of the stolen jewellery. What evidentiary principle applies?
record.expected_answer: Recent unexplained possession of stolen property lets the court presume the possessor is the thief or receiver. The photos are electronic evidence (Section 63 BSA certificate needed); the recovered jewellery itself should be seized under a memo and identified by the owner.

question: What can I do if my fundamental rights are violated?
response: Under Section 13 of the Constitution of India (Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part), the State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void. record.question: What can I do if my fundamental rights are violated?

question: What is a writ of habeas corpus?
response: Under Section 139 of the Constitution of India (Conferment on the Supreme Court of powers to issue certain writs), Parliament may by law confer on the Supreme Court power to issue directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for any purposes other than those mentioned in clause (2) of article 32. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is a writ of habeas corpus?
record.expected_answer: Habeas corpus ('produce the body') commands whoever detains a person to bring them before the court and justify the detention; if it is illegal, the person is freed. It is the primary remedy against unlawful detention, available even against private persons.

question: What is the writ of mandamus used for?
response: Under Section 139 of the Constitution of India (Conferment on the Supreme Court of powers to issue certain writs), the Supreme Court may issue writs in the nature of mandamus, certiorari, prohibition and quo warranto. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the writ of mandamus used for?
record.expected_answer: Mandamus commands a public authority to perform a public legal duty it has failed or refused to perform — e.g. directing a municipal body to act on a licence application. It does not lie against private individuals or purely discretionary functions.

question: What rights does Article 22 give an arrested person?
response: Under Section 22 of the Constitution of India (Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases), no person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice. record.question: What rights does Article 22 give an arrested person?
record.expected_answer: Article 22 guarantees the right to be informed of grounds of arrest, to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice, and production before a Magistrate within 24 hours — beyond which detention needs judicial authority. Preventive detention has separate, narrower safeguards.

question: What is Article 20's protection against double jeopardy?
response: Under Section 20 of the Constitution of India (Protection in respect of conviction for offences), no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the Act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is Article 20's protection against double jeopardy?

question: What is the 'basic structure' doctrine?
response: Under Section 143 of the Constitution of India, the basic structure doctrine refers to the fundamental principles of liberty, equality, and fraternity which cannot be altered by the legislature. record.question: What is the 'basic structure' doctrine?
record.expected_answer: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court held Parliament can amend the Constitution under Article 368 but cannot destroy its basic structure — features like supremacy of the Constitution, judicial review, secularism, federalism, and free and fair elections.

question: Are Supreme Court judgments binding on all courts?
response: Under Section 141 of the Constitution of India (Law declared by Supreme Court to be binding on all courts), the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India. record.question: Are Supreme Court judgments binding on all courts?

question: Who can grant pardons for death sentences?

question: Are non-citizens protected by Indian fundamental rights?
response: Under Section 8 of the Constitution of India (Rights of citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India), notwithstanding anything in article 5, any person who or either of whose parents or any of whose grand-parents was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted), and who is ordinarily residing in any country outside India as so defined shall be deemed to be a citizen of India if he has been registered as a citizen of India by the diplomatic or consular representative of India in the country where he is for the time being residing on an application made by him therefor to such diplomatic or consular representative, whether before or after the commencement of this Constitution, in the form and manner prescribed by the Government of the Dominion of India or the Government of India. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Are non-citizens protected by Indian fundamental rights?
record.expected_answer: Partially. Rights like Articles 14, 20, 21 and 22 protect 'persons' — including foreigners; rights like Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29-30 are for citizens only. So a foreigner gets fair procedure and equality but not, e.g., free speech under 19.

question: What is Article 15(3) and why does it matter for women?
response: Under Article 15(3) of the Constitution of India, the State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them. This is important for women because it prohibits discrimination against women on grounds of sex, which includes marital rape, denial of education, and other forms of gender-based violence.

record.question: What is Article 15(3) and why does it matter for women?
record.expected_answer: Article 15(3) lets the State make special provisions for women and children notwithstanding the non-discrimination rule — the constitutional foundation for laws like the DV Act, maternity benefits, and reserved seats in local bodies.

quarantined_facts.fact: special provisions for women and children valid

question: Can the government take my land for a project?
response: Under Section 31A of the Constitution of India (Saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates, etc), notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law providing for the acquisition by the State of any estate or of any rights therein or the extinguishment or modification of any such rights, or the taking over of the management of any property by the State for a limited period either in the public interest or in order to secure the proper management of the property, or the extinguishment or modification of any rights of managing agents, secretaries and treasurers, managing directors, directors or managers of corporations, or of any voting rights of shareholders thereof, or the saving of certain laws, the executive power of the Union and of each State shall extend to the carrying on of any trade or business and to the acquisition, holding and disposal of property and the making of contracts for any purpose. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can the government take my land for a project?
record.expected_answer: Yes, but only by authority of law (Article 300A) — under the Land Acquisition Act, 2013 (RFCTLARR), which requires public purpose, social impact assessment, consent thresholds for private/PPP projects, and compensation up to 2x (urban) or 4x (rural) market value, plus rehabilitation.

question: What are the Panchayati Raj provisions in the Constitution?
response: Under Section 243B of the Constitution of India (Constitution of Panchayats), there shall be constituted in every State, Panchayats at the village, intermediate and district levels in accordance with the provisions of this Part. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What are the Panchayati Raj provisions in the Constitution?
record.expected_answer: The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) added Parts IX and IXA — constitutional status for panchayats and municipalities, regular five-year elections, one-third reservation for women (many states now 50%), SC/ST reservation, and State Election/Finance Commissions.

question: Who decides disputes about the election of the President of India?
response: Under Section 71 of the Constitution of India (Matters relating to, or connected with, the election of a President or Vice-President), all doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of a President or Vice-President shall be inquired into and decided by the Supreme Court whose decision shall be final. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Who decides disputes about the election of the President of India?
record.expected_answer: Only the Supreme Court, under Article 71 — doubts and disputes about the election of the President or Vice-President are inquired into and decided exclusively by the Supreme Court.

question: What is judicial review?
response: Under Section 137 of the Constitution of India (Review of judgments or orders by the Supreme Court), the Supreme Court shall have power to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is judicial review?
record.expected_answer: Judicial review is the courts' power to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution and strike down what violates it — grounded in Articles 13, 32, 226. It is part of the basic structure and cannot be excluded.

question: The state passed a law taking away a fundamental right. Is the law automatically void?
response: Under Section 13 of the Constitution of India (Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights), (1) All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: The state passed a law taking away a fundamental right. Is the law automatically void?
record.expected_answer: Under Article 13, laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void to the extent of inconsistency — but a court must declare it; until struck down the law operates. Constitutional amendments are tested on the basic-structure standard instead.
required_facts: Article 13 void to extent of inconsistency

question: Do I have a fundamental right to travel abroad?
response: Under Section 32 of the Constitution of India (Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part), the right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed. This is a fundamental right, but it does not cover travelling abroad. Consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Do I have a fundamental right to travel abroad?
record.expected_answer: Yes — the right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Article 21 (Satwant Singh; Maneka Gandhi). A passport can be impounded only by fair procedure under the Passports Act with reasons and hearing.

question: What is a 'money bill' and why was Aadhaar's passage controversial?
response: Under Section 109 of the Constitution of India (Special procedure in respect of Money Bills), a Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential. Under Section 198 of the Constitution of India (Special procedure in respect of Money Bills), (1) A Money Bill shall not be introduced in a Legislative Council. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential. The Aadhaar Act was passed as a Money Bill despite opposition from several MPs, including the Leader of Opposition, because the government claimed it was necessary for national security and economic development. This was controversial because Money Bills are supposed to relate to taxation, borrowing, or the appropriation of money, and the Aadhaar scheme did not meet this criterion. The Supreme Court later ruled that the Aadhaar Act could not be treated as a Money Bill, and the government had to seek approval from Parliament through a Resolution instead. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is a 'money bill' and why was Aadhaar's passage controversial?
record.expected_answer: A money bill (Article 110) deals only with taxation, government borrowing/spending and related matters, and needs only Lok Sabha approval — Rajya Sabha can merely recommend. Aadhaar Act's passage as a money bill was challenged; the majority in Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) upheld it, with the Speaker's certification held reviewable.

question: Which article deals with uniform civil code?
response: Under Section 44 of the Constitution of India (Uniform civil code for the citizens), the State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Which article deals with uniform civil code?
record.expected_answer: Article 44, a Directive Principle, directs the State to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code. It is not enforceable by courts; personal laws continue unless replaced by legislation (some states have enacted their own UCC laws).

question: Are linguistic minorities protected?
response: Under Section 29 of the Constitution of India (Protection of interests of minorities), (1) Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Are linguistic minorities protected?
record.expected_answer: Yes. Articles 29-30 protect minorities' rights to conserve their language, script and culture and to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice; Article 350A/350B address mother-tongue instruction and a Special Officer for linguistic minorities.

question: Can the police restrict a peaceful protest?
response: Under Section 148 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force), when the public security is manifestly endangered by any such assembly and no Executive Magistrate can be communicated with, any commissioned or gazetted officer of the armed forces may disperse such assembly with the help of the armed forces under his command, and may arrest and confine any persons forming part of it, in order to disperse such assembly or that they may be punished according to law. This is legal restriction on peaceful protest, but only in extreme circumstances. Otherwise, the police must allow peaceful assembly.

record.question: Can the police restrict a peaceful protest?
record.expected_answer: Peaceful assembly without arms is a fundamental right (Article 19(1)(b)) subject to reasonable restrictions for public order — permissions, route conditions, or prohibitory orders under Section 163 BNSS. Blanket or indefinite bans are disproportionate; occupation of public ways indefinitely is not protected (Shaheen Bagh ruling).

question: What is the collegium system?
response: Under this system, the appointment, transfer, suspension, resignation, removal, and conditions of service of judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts are governed by the Constitution itself and no law can be passed in this regard. This is known as the collegium system. Section 203 of the Constitution of India. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the collegium system?
record.expected_answer: The collegium is the judge-led appointment mechanism from the Second and Third Judges cases: the CJI and senior-most SC judges recommend appointments/transfers of SC and HC judges, with primacy over the executive. The NJAC alternative was struck down in 2015 for violating judicial independence.

question: What protection do government employees have against arbitrary dismissal?
response: Under Section 311 of the Constitution of India (Dismissal, removal or reduction in rank of persons employed in civil capacities under the Union or a State), no person who is a member of a civil service of the Union or an all-India service or a civil service of a State or holds a civil post under the Union or a State shall be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What protection do government employees have against arbitrary dismissal?
record.expected_answer: Article 311 protects civil servants: no dismissal by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority, and no dismissal/removal/reduction in rank without an inquiry with notice and opportunity to be heard (with narrow exceptions like conviction or security of state).
required_facts: inquiry and opportunity to be heard

question: Can a state law and central law conflict? Which wins?
response: Under Section 254 of the Constitution of India (Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States), if any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List, then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, or, as the case may be, the existing law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can a state law and central law conflict? Which wins?
record.expected_answer: In the Concurrent List, the central law prevails to the extent of repugnancy (Article 254); a conflicting state law survives only with Presidential assent, and even then Parliament can override. In exclusive fields, the legislature with competence prevails.
required_facts: central law prevails in Concurrent List

question: Does the Constitution guarantee equal pay for equal work?
response: Under Section 39A of the Constitution of India (Equal justice and free legal aid), the State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Does the Constitution guarantee equal pay for equal work?
record.expected_answer: Equal pay for equal work is a Directive Principle (Article 39(d)) read with Articles 14-16 into an enforceable principle in appropriate cases — the Supreme Court has applied it to temporary employees performing identical duties (State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh, 2016).

question: What remedy exists against custodial torture?
response: Under Section 323 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Torture), whoever causes torture shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What remedy exists against custodial torture?
record.expected_answer: Custodial violence violates Article 21. Remedies: habeas corpus/writ petitions, constitutional compensation (Nilabati Behera; DK Basu guidelines now largely codified), complaints to the NHRC/SHRC, mandatory magisterial inquiry in custodial deaths, and prosecution of the officers. Medical examination records are key evidence.

question: Which constitutional functionary decides whether a bill is a money bill?
response: Under Section 199 of the Constitution of India (Definition of "Money Bills"), (1) For the purposes of this Chapter, a Bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with all or any of the following matters, namely:— (a) the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax; (3) If any question arises whether a Bill introduced in the Legislature of a State which has a Legislative Council is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of such State thereon shall be final. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Which constitutional functionary decides whether a bill is a money bill?
record.expected_answer: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha certifies whether a bill is a money bill under Article 110(3). The certification was traditionally final, but the Supreme Court has held it is open to judicial review in appropriate cases.

question: Which law protects consumers in India and when was it enacted?
response: Under Section 10 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Establishment of Central Consumer Protection Authority), this Act came into force on 15-12-2019. This is a law protecting consumers in India, enacted on 15-12-2019.

record.question: Which law protects consumers in India and when was it enacted?
record.expected_answer: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (in force from July 2020) protects consumers, replacing the 1986 Act. It covers goods and services including e-commerce, and created the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA).

question: Where do I file a consumer complaint for a defective Rs 30,000 phone?
response: Under Section 34 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Jurisdiction of District Commission), the District Commission shall have jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed one crore rupees. This covers your Rs 30,000 phone, so you can file with a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the opposite party or each of the opposite parties, where there are more than one, at the time of the institution of the complaint, ordinarily resides or carries on business or has a branch office or personally works for gain. The official guidance is to file with a District Commission.

record.question: Where do I file a consumer complaint for a defective Rs 30,000 phone?
record.expected_answer: Before the District Consumer Commission — it handles complaints where the consideration paid is up to Rs 50 lakh. You can file where you reside or work, not just where the seller is, and online via the e-daakhil portal. For Rs 30,000, engage no lawyer if you prefer; the process is designed to be consumer-friendly.
required_facts: District Commission up to Rs 50 lakh

question: What are the money limits for District, State and National Consumer Commissions?
response: Under Section 34 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Jurisdiction of District Commission), the District Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed one crore rupees. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What are the money limits for District, State and National Consumer Commissions?
record.expected_answer: Under the 2021 Rules: District Commission — consideration paid up to Rs 50 lakh; State Commission — above Rs 50 lakh up to Rs 2 crore; National Commission — above Rs 2 crore. Jurisdiction is based on the amount actually paid, not the compensation claimed.
forbidden_facts: one crore limit for District Commission (pre-2021)

question: Can I file a consumer case against an e-commerce platform for a fake product sold by a third-party seller?
response: Under Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Manner in which complaint shall be made), a complaint, in relation to any goods sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or any service provided or agreed to be provided, may be filed with a District Commission by the consumer, to whom such goods are sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or such service is provided or agreed to be provided. This covers filing against a third-party seller, but not an e-commerce platform itself. The platform is liable only if it fails to take reasonable care to prevent the sale of counterfeit goods, which is separate from the consumer's right to compensation for harm caused by a defective product. Consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can I file a consumer case against an e-commerce platform for a fake product sold by a third-party seller?
record.expected_answer: Yes. The CPA 2019 and the E-Commerce Rules, 2020 cover marketplaces: platforms must disclose seller details, honour returns/refunds, and can be liable for failing their duties or for unfair trade practices. Complain to the platform's grievance officer first, then the Consumer Commission or the National Consumer Helpline (1915).

question: What is 'deficiency in service'?
response: Under Section 318 of the Constitution of India (Power to make regulations as to conditions of service of members and staff of the Commission), the power to make regulations as to conditions of service of members and staff of the Commission is given to the President and, in the case of a State Commission, the Governor *** of the State. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is 'deficiency in service'?
record.expected_answer: Deficiency is any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality or manner of service required by law or contract — including negligence causing loss and deliberate withholding of information. It grounds compensation claims before Consumer Commissions.

question: The builder is 3 years late delivering my flat. Can I go to the consumer forum, or only RERA?
response: Under Indian law, Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers manner in which complaint shall be made — this is separate from RERA, which applies to builders. You can file a complaint under this section, but first check the limit of Rs 1 crore per complaint (Section 34). Approach the District Commission, or file electronically if permitted (Section 35). This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: The builder is 3 years late delivering my flat. Can I go to the consumer forum, or only RERA?
record.expected_answer: Both remedies exist — a homebuyer is a consumer and can choose the Consumer Commission or RERA (they are concurrent, per Supreme Court rulings); pick one forum for the same relief. RERA offers interest for delay and project oversight; consumer forums offer refund/compensation. Check your paid amount for the right commission tier.
required_facts: consumer forum and RERA are concurrent remedies

question: My insurance claim was rejected citing a technicality after hospital discharge. What can I do?
response: Under Section 163 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (Refund in certain cases of compensation paid under section 161), when any compensation or other amount in lieu of or by way of satisfaction of a claim for compensation is awarded or paid in respect of such death or grievous hurt under any other provision of this Act or any other law for the time being in force or otherwise, so much of the other compensation or other amount aforesaid as is equal to the compensation paid under section 161, shall be refunded to the insurer. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My insurance claim was rejected citing a technicality after hospital discharge. What can I do?
record.expected_answer: First use the insurer's grievance process, then escalate to the Insurance Ombudsman (free, for claims up to Rs 50 lakh) or file before the Consumer Commission for deficiency in service within two years. Wrongful repudiation is routinely compensated; keep the policy, rejection letter and medical papers.

question: What is product liability under the CPA 2019?
response: Under Section 83 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Product liability action), a product liability action may be brought by a complainant against a product manufacturer or a product service provider or a product seller, as the case may be, for any harm caused to him on account of a defective product. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is product liability under the CPA 2019?
record.expected_answer: A statutory claim for harm caused by a defective product — against the manufacturer (defects, deviation from specs, inadequate warnings), the service provider, or even the seller in specified cases. Harm includes injury, property damage and mental agony; contract disclaimers cannot defeat it.
required_facts: claim for harm from defective product

quarantined_facts.fact: manufacturer, service provider or seller liable

question: A hospital's negligence during surgery injured my wife. Is medical negligence a consumer matter?
response: Under Indian law, medical negligence is not covered under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Section 81 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019). This is a consumer protection act, and medical negligence falls under the scope of the Medical Council of India and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 applies to goods and services, not medical malpractice. Consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: A hospital's negligence during surgery injured my wife. Is medical negligence a consumer matter?
record.expected_answer: Yes. Paid medical services are 'services' under the CPA (Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha), so negligence claims lie before Consumer Commissions — choose the tier by the amount paid; large compensation claims are often filed with expert medical evidence. Criminal negligence prosecution and Medical Council complaints are separate tracks.

question: Do I need a lawyer for a consumer complaint?
response: Under Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Manner in which complaint shall be made), a complaint relating to violation of consumer rights or unfair trade practices or false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of consumers as a class, may be forwarded either in writing or in electronic mode, to any one of the authorities, namely, the District Collector or the Commissioner of regional office or the Central Authority. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Do I need a lawyer for a consumer complaint?
record.expected_answer: No. Consumer Commissions are designed for self-representation: file on e-daakhil with your complaint, bills, correspondence and affidavit; fees are nominal (nil for claims up to Rs 5 lakh). Hearings are relatively informal, and many consumers argue their own cases.
required_facts: no fee up to Rs 5 lakh

question: What is the National Consumer Helpline number?
response: The National Consumer Helpline number is 1915 (toll-free) or +91-88000-01915 (WhatsApp). This is the National Consumer Helpline run by the Department of Consumer Affairs to help consumers register grievances, get guidance, and track resolution — it also offers a web portal, mobile app and the UMANG app. This is official guidance.

record.question: What is the National Consumer Helpline number?
record.expected_answer: 1915 — the National Consumer Helpline (also via the INGRAM portal/app), which registers grievances and takes them up with companies through convergence; it is a pre-litigation step, not a court.

question: Can consumer disputes be settled by mediation?
response: Under Section 37 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Reference to mediation), at the first hearing of the complaint after its admission, or at any later stage, if it appears to the District Commission that there exists elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, except in such cases as may be prescribed, it may direct the parties to give in writing, within five days, consent to have their dispute settled by mediation in accordance with the provisions of Chapter V. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can consumer disputes be settled by mediation?
record.expected_answer: Yes. The CPA 2019 created consumer mediation cells attached to each Commission; with both parties' consent the Commission refers the dispute to mediation, and a settlement so reached is final with no appeal.

question: What can the Consumer Commission actually order in my favour?
response: Under Section 41 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Appeal against order of District Commission), an appeal against an order made by the District Commission may be preferred to the State Commission on the grounds of facts or law within a period of forty-five days from the date of the order. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What can the Consumer Commission actually order in my favour?
record.expected_answer: Removal of defects, replacement, refund with interest, compensation for loss and mental agony, litigation costs, discontinuation of unfair practices, and withdrawal of hazardous goods. Orders are enforceable like court decrees — non-compliance can bring imprisonment and fines.

question: I lost in the District Commission. Can I appeal?
response: Under Section 41 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Appeal against order of District Commission), any person aggrieved by an order made by the District Commission may prefer an appeal against such order to the State Commission on the grounds of facts or law within a period of forty-five days from the date of the order, in such form and manner, as may be prescribed. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: I lost in the District Commission. Can I appeal?
record.expected_answer: Yes — to the State Commission within 45 days (condonable), with a statutory deposit of 50% of any amount ordered against you. Further appeals: State to National Commission, and on to the Supreme Court, each with deposit/limitation rules.
required_facts: appeal to State Commission within 45 days

question: Is a free service covered under consumer law?
response: Under Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Manner in which complaint shall be made), a complaint, in relation to any goods sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or any service provided or agreed to be provided, may be filed with a District Commission by— (a) the consumer,— (i) to whom such goods are sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or such service is provided or agreed to be provided; or (ii) who alleges unfair trade practice in respect of such goods or service; (b) any recognised consumer association, whether the consumer to whom such goods are sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or such service is provided or agreed to be provided, or who alleges unfair trade practice in respect of such goods or service, is a member of such association or not; (c) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest, with the permission of the District Commission, on behalf of, or for the benefit of, all consumers so interested; or (d) the Central Government, the Central Authority or the State Government, as the case may be: Provided that the complaint under this sub-section may be filed electronically in such manner as may be prescribed. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Is a free service covered under consumer law?
record.expected_answer: No. Services rendered free of charge are excluded — you must have paid (or promised) consideration to be a 'consumer'. But 'free' gifts tied to purchases, and government hospital services where some patients pay, have nuanced treatment in case law.

question: Are goods bought for business/resale covered by consumer law?
response: Under Section 6 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Goods bought for business or resale), no consumer right shall apply to goods bought for business or resale. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Are goods bought for business/resale covered by consumer law?
record.expected_answer: No — persons buying goods for resale or commercial purposes are not 'consumers'. Exception: goods bought for self-employment to earn livelihood (e.g. an auto-rickshaw driven by the buyer) still qualify.

question: The restaurant charged a 'service charge' automatically. Is that allowed?
response: Under Section 6A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Delivery of services by service provider), when the manner of committing offence must be stated. Charges may be collected by service providers under this section notwithstanding the fact that there is no express provision under the Act, rule, regulation or notification under which the service is provided to collect, retain and appropriate e-service charges by the service providers. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: The restaurant charged a 'service charge' automatically. Is that allowed?
record.expected_answer: Automatic/compulsory service charge is prohibited by CCPA guidelines (2022) — it must be voluntary, and menus/bills cannot disguise it as tax. Refuse to pay it, complain on 1915, or file before the Commission; the Delhi High Court has upheld the CCPA's guidelines.
required_facts: CCPA 2022 guidelines prohibit compulsory service charge

question: What is the CCPA and how is it different from consumer courts?
response: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) is an independent body established under Section 16 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. It is different from consumer courts, which are district-level tribunals set up under Section 33 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The CCPA can direct the advertiser, manufacturer, endorser or publisher to discontinue or modify a false or misleading advertisement, and can impose penalties up to two years' imprisonment and Rs 10 lakh fine for a first offence, rising for repeat offences.

record.question: What is the CCPA and how is it different from consumer courts?
record.expected_answer: The Central Consumer Protection Authority is a regulator (not a court) that protects consumers as a class — investigating violations, recalling unsafe goods, ordering refunds, penalising misleading ads. Consumer Commissions adjudicate individual disputes; the CCPA acts suo motu or on complaints.

question: My new car turned out to have a manufacturing defect the dealer can't fix. What am I entitled to?
response: Under Section 84 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Liability of product manufacturer), a product manufacturer shall be liable in a product liability action, if the product contains a manufacturing defect. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My new car turned out to have a manufacturing defect the dealer can't fix. What am I entitled to?
record.expected_answer: Replacement of the vehicle or refund of the price with compensation — Commissions regularly order these for irreparable manufacturing defects, against both manufacturer and dealer. Keep job cards showing repeated failed repairs; the amount paid decides the forum tier.
required_facts: replacement or refund for manufacturing defect

question: Are coaching institutes accountable if they promise '100% selection' falsely?
response: Under Section 69 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment), whoever intends to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, voluntarily conceals by any act or omission, or by the use of encryption or any other information hiding tool, the existence of a design to commit such offence or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years. This covers false promises of selection, among other things. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Are coaching institutes accountable if they promise '100% selection' falsely?
record.expected_answer: Yes. False success-rate claims are misleading advertisements — the CCPA has penalised coaching institutes and issued guidelines (2024) against misleading coaching ads; students can also claim refunds for deficiency. question: What is the punishment for cyber terrorism?
response: Under Section 66F of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Punishment for cyber terrorism), (1) Whoever,– (A) with intent to threaten the unity, integrity, security or sovereignty of India or to strike terror in the people or any section of the people by– (i) denying or cause the denial of access to any person authorised to access computer resource; or (ii) attempting to penetrate or access a computer resource without authorisation or exceeding authorised access; or (iii) introducing or causing to introduce any computer contaminant, and by means of such conduct causes or is likely to cause death or injuries to persons or damage to or destruction of property or disrupts or knowing that it is likely to cause damage or disruption of supplies or services essential to the life of the community or adversely affect the critical information infrastructure specified under section 70; or (B) knowingly or intentionally penetrates or accesses a computer resource without authorisation or exceeding authorised access, and by means of such conduct obtains access to information, data or computer data base that is restricted for reasons of the security of the State or foreign relations; or any restricted information, data or computer data base, with reasons to believe that such information, data or computer data base so obtained may be used to cause or likely to cause injury to the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence, or to the advantage of any foreign nation, group of individuals or otherwise, commits the offence of cyber terrorism. This is punishable with imprisonment which may extend to imprisonment for life. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the punishment for cyber terrorism?
record.expected_answer: Section 66F IT Act punishes cyber terrorism — attacks on critical systems or unauthorised access threatening India's unity, security — with imprisonment which may extend to life. BNS 113 (terrorist act) can also apply.

question: Someone is running a Telegram group selling exam papers and my details were leaked there. What offences arise?

record.question: Someone is running a Telegram group selling exam papers and my details were leaked there. What offences arise?

question: What should I preserve as evidence after an online fraud?
response: Under Section 66B of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Punishment for dishonestly receiving stolen computer resource or communication device), when a person dishonestly receives or retains any stolen computer resource or communication device knowing or having reason to believe the same to be stolen computer resource or communication device, they shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may extend to rupees one lakh or with both. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What should I preserve as evidence after an online fraud?
record.expected_answer: Screenshots with URLs and timestamps, transaction IDs/UTRs and bank statements, the fraudster's numbers/UPI IDs/profiles, call recordings, emails with full headers, and the devices themselves unaltered. These become electronic evidence under Section 63 BSA — the complaint on cybercrime.gov.in generates an acknowledgement number to keep.

question: An unknown person is using my photo on a matrimonial site. Which remedy applies?
response: Under Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Punishment for cheating by personation by using computer resource), whoever, by means of any communication device or computer resource cheats by personation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to one lakh rupees. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: An unknown person is using my photo on a matrimonial site. Which remedy applies?

question: Can WhatsApp be forced to reveal who sent a message?
response: Under Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Punishment for sending offensive messages through communication service, etc), no. The Court may presume that an electronic message, forwarded by the originator through an electronic mail server to the addressee to whom the message purports to be addressed corresponds with the message as fed into his computer for transmission; but the Court shall not make any presumption as to the person by whom such message was sent. record.question: Can WhatsApp be forced to reveal who sent a message?

question: What is 'sextortion' and what should a victim never do?
response: Under Section 308 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Extortion), sextortion is when someone threatens to share intimate images or videos of you unless you pay money or send more content; it is criminal extortion. record.question: What is 'sextortion' and what should a victim never do?

record.question: Are cryptocurrency frauds covered by Indian law?

record.question: What legal duties do companies have when hit by ransomware affecting customer data?

question: How do I get a scam website blocked?
response: Under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Power to issue directions for blocking for public access of any information through any computer resource), the Central Government or any of its officers specially authorised by it in this behalf is satisfied that it is necessary or expedient so to do, in the interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence relating to above, it may subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), for reasons to be recorded in writing, by order, direct any agency of the Government or intermediary to block for access by the public or cause to be blocked for access by the public any information generated, transmitted, received, stored or hosted in any computer resource. record.question: How do I get a scam website blocked?
record.expected_answer: Report it on cybercrime.gov.in (I4C coordinates blocking through MeitY under Section 69A IT Act) and to the registrar/host via WHOIS abuse contacts; banks/payment gateways can blacklist its merchant accounts. CERT-In and RBI also act on phishing domains reported to them.

question: Can I record a phone call I am part of, and use it later?
response: Under Section 132 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Professional communications), no advocate, shall at any time be permitted, unless with his client's express consent, to disclose any communication made to him in the course and for the purpose of his service as such advocate, by or on behalf of his client, or to state the contents or condition of any document with which he has become acquainted in the course and for the purpose of his professional service, or to disclose any advice given by him to his client in the course and for the purpose of such service. record.question: Can I record a phone call I am part of, and use it later?
record.expected_answer: Recording a call you are a party to is generally lawful and such recordings are admissible (electronic record with Section 63 BSA certificate), subject to relevance — though spousal secret recordings raise privacy tensions courts are still working out. Tapping others' calls without authorisation is illegal (Telegraph/IT Act).

question: What is the IT Rules 2021 grievance mechanism on social media?
response: Under Section 90 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Power of State Government to make rules), the Controller shall publish notice of such suspension or revocation, as the case may be, in all such repositories. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the IT Rules 2021 grievance mechanism on social media?
record.expected_answer: Every significant platform must appoint an India-based Grievance Officer (acknowledge complaints in 24 hours, resolve in 15 days; 72 hours for certain content), a Chief Compliance Officer and a Nodal Officer. Users unhappy with the platform's decision can appeal to the government-appointed Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) within 30 days.

question: Fraudsters used my Aadhaar to open a bank account. What should I do?
response: Under Section 133 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, whoever fraudulently obtains or uses any document, electronic record or public key, knowing or having reason to believe that such document, electronic record or public key is false or fictitious, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. This covers the use of your Aadhaar to open a bank account. File a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in, get a complaint reference number, and file a FIR with the local police station. Inform the RBI and the bank where the account was opened about the fraud. The official guidance is to file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in.

record.question: Fraudsters used my Aadhaar to open a bank account. What should I do?
record.expected_answer: Lock your Aadhaar biometrics on myAadhaar, get the account details via the bank/AEPS trail, file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in and an FIR (identity theft 66C IT Act, cheating 318 BNS), inform UIDAI, and dispute any loans via the credit bureaus. Banks must reverse fraudulent AEPS debits reported promptly under RBI rules.

question: How do I file an RTI application and what does it cost?
response: Under Section 6 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Request for obtaining information), a person may make a request in writing or through electronic means in English or Hindi or in the official language of the area in which the application is being made, accompanying such fee as may be prescribed, to the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, of the concerned public authority. The fee for requests to central government authorities is Rs 10, payable in cash, by demand draft/banker's cheque/postal order, or electronically where the authority permits. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: How do I file an RTI application and what does it cost?
record.expected_answer: Write a simple application (no format required) to the Public Information Officer of the department, pay Rs 10 (for central bodies; states vary) — BPL applicants pay nothing — and submit in person, by post, or online at rtionline.gov.in for central ministries. No reasons need be given for seeking information.

question: Within how many days must an RTI application be answered?
response: Under Section 7 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Time limit for providing information), an application for information shall be dealt with by the Public Information Officer within thirty days of the receipt of the application. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Within how many days must an RTI application be answered?
record.expected_answer: 30 days from receipt (35 if filed with an Assistant PIO), and just 48 hours where the information concerns life or liberty. If transferred to another authority, 5 days are added. Deemed refusal after the deadline lets you appeal.

question: The PIO ignored my RTI application. What is my remedy?
response: Under Section 9 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Grounds for rejection to access in certain cases), the PIO may reject a request for information where such a request for providing access would involve an infringement of copyright subsisting in a person other than the State. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: The PIO ignored my RTI application. What is my remedy?
record.expected_answer: File a first appeal to the First Appellate Authority (senior officer in the same department) within 30 days of the deadline/response. If still unsatisfied, file a second appeal to the Central/State Information Commission within 90 days. No fee for central first appeals; the Commission can order disclosure and penalise the PIO.

question: Can a PIO be punished for wrongly denying information?
response: Under Section 20 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Penalties), (1)Where the Central Information Commission or the State Information Commission, as the case may be, at the time of deciding any complaint or appeal is of the opinion that the Central Public Information Officer or the State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, has, without any reasonable cause, refused to receive an application for information or has not furnished information within the time specified under sub-section (1) of section 7 or malafidely denied the request for information or knowingly given incorrect, incomplete or misleading information or destroyed information which was the subject of the request or obstructed in any manner in furnishing the information, it shall impose a penalty of two hundred and fifty rupees each day till application is received or information is furnished, so however, the total amount of such penalty shall not exceed twenty-five thousand rupees: Provided that the Central Public Information Officer or the State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before any penalty is imposed on him: Provided further that the burden of proving that he acted reasonably and diligently shall be on the Central Public Information Officer or the State Public Information Officer, as the case may be. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can a PIO be punished for wrongly denying information?
record.expected_answer: Yes. The Information Commission can impose a penalty of Rs 250 per day of delay up to Rs 25,000 on the PIO for malafide denial, knowingly wrong information or destruction of records, and recommend disciplinary action; compensation to the applicant can also be ordered.

question: What information can the government refuse to give under RTI?
response: Under Section 8 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Exemption from disclosure of information), information, disclosure of which would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security, strategic, scientific or economic interests of the State, relation with foreign State or lead to incitement of an offence is exempt. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What information can the government refuse to give under RTI?
record.expected_answer: Section 8 exemptions: national security/sovereignty, forbidden by courts, breach of parliamentary privilege, commercial confidence/trade secrets, fiduciary relationships, foreign government confidences, endangering life/safety of informants, investigation impediments, cabinet papers (till decision taken), and unwarranted invasion of personal privacy — but disclosure prevails if public interest outweighs the harm (s.8(2)). Most exemptions lapse after 20 years.

question: Can I ask for file notings and officers' names under RTI?

This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can I ask for file notings and officers' names under RTI?
record.expected_answer: Yes — file notings are 'information' and disclosable (CIC has held so consistently), including names/designations of officers on the file, unless a specific Section 8 exemption applies to the content.

question: Does RTI apply to private companies?
response: Under Section 8 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Information which is exempt from being made available under this Act), information affecting India's sovereignty, security, strategic, scientific or economic interests, or relations with foreign states is exempt. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Does RTI apply to private companies?
record.expected_answer: Not directly — RTI covers 'public authorities' (government bodies and those substantially financed/controlled by government). question: Can I find out the status of my pending government application (pension, licence) through RTI?
response: Under Section 10 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Status of application), a public authority shall inform the applicant of the status of his application within thirty days of receipt of the application. This covers applications for pension, licences etc., but you should check specifically whether the authority is covered by the RTI Act — many government departments are exempt. You cannot use the RTI portal for applications like these, you must file directly with the department concerned.

record.question: Can I find out the status of my pending government application (pension, licence) through RTI?
record.expected_answer: Yes — this is one of RTI's most effective uses: ask for the current status, file movement, officer responsible, and the prescribed timeline for disposal. Such RTIs often unblock stuck files; cite the department's citizen charter timelines.

question: Can I get copies of my own answer sheet from a public exam under RTI?
response: Under Section 8 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Right to inspect and copy documents), any person has a right to inspect and copy any document held by a public authority. This covers your answer sheet from a public exam, but you must approach the appropriate public authority directly rather than filing an RTI request. The RTI Act applies to information held by public authorities, not to individual documents like exam answer sheets.

record.question: Can I get copies of my own answer sheet from a public exam under RTI?
record.expected_answer: Yes. The Supreme Court in CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011) held evaluated answer sheets are information accessible under RTI, subject to reasonable fees; examiner identities can be masked.

question: Are BPL applicants really exempt from all RTI fees?

record.question: Are BPL applicants really exempt from all RTI fees?

question: Can I ask under RTI why my neighbour got a government contract?

question: What is the third-party procedure in RTI?
response: Under Section 11 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Third party information), (1) Where a Central Public Information Officer or a State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, intends to disclose any information or record, or part thereof on a request made under this Act, which relates to or has been supplied by a third party and has been treated as confidential by that third party, the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, shall, within five days from the receipt of the request, give a written notice to such third party of the request and of the fact that the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, intends to disclose the information or record, or part thereof, and invite the third party to make a submission in writing or orally, regarding whether the information should be disclosed, and such submission of the third party shall be kept in view while taking a decision about disclosure of information: Provided that except in the case of trade or commercial secrets protected by law, disclosure may be allowed if the public interest in disclosure outweighs in importance any possible harm or injury to the interests of such third party. record.question: What is the third-party procedure in RTI?
record.expected_answer: If requested information relates to or was supplied by a third party who treated it as confidential, the PIO must notify that party within 5 days; the party has 10 days to object, and the PIO then decides weighing public interest — with disclosure timelines extended to 40 days.

question: Can RTI be filed in Hindi or regional languages?
response: Under Section 6 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Filing of request for information), any person may file a request in English, Hindi or the language used in the area in which the public authority is located. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can RTI be filed in Hindi or regional languages?

question: How do I file RTI for a state government department online?
response: Under Indian law, Section 64 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 covers summons how served, which is not directly relevant to filing an RTI request. RTI requests for state government departments are typically filed physically or by post to the concerned PIO, not online. The RTI Online portal (rtionline.gov.in) is for central government bodies only. For state government departments, use the state's own RTI portal (if available) or file physically/by post to that authority's PIO. There is no timeline given here — filing an RTI request usually takes several working days, depending on the department's processing time.

record.question: How do I file RTI for a state government department online?
record.expected_answer: Use that state's RTI portal if it has one (many states run their own; rtionline.gov.in covers only central bodies) — otherwise post the application with the state-prescribed fee (often Rs 10, payable by IPO/DD/court-fee stamp per state rules) to the department's PIO.

question: What happens to my RTI if the PIO says the record was destroyed?
response: Under Section 7 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Information in cognizable cases), where the Central Information Commission or the State Information Commission, as the case may be, at the time of deciding any complaint or appeal is of the opinion that the Central Public Information Officer or the State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, has, without any reasonable cause and persistently, failed to receive an application for information or has not furnished information within the time specified under sub-section (1) of section 7 or malafidely denied the request for information or knowingly given incorrect, incomplete or misleading information or destroyed information which was the subject of the request or obstructed in any manner in furnishing the information, it shall recommend for disciplinary action against the Central Public Information Officer or the State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, under the service rules applicable to him. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What happens to my RTI if the PIO says the record was destroyed?
record.expected_answer: Ask for the record-retention schedule and destruction certificate — destruction contrary to retention rules, or after your RTI was filed, invites penalties and even prosecution under records laws. The Commission can direct reconstruction where feasible and penalise malafide destruction.

question: Can I seek reasons for an administrative decision that affected me?
response: Under Section 19 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Appeal), any person who, does not receive a decision within the time specified in sub-section (1) or clause (a) of sub-section (3) of section 7, or is aggrieved by a decision of the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, may within thirty days from the expiry of such period or from the receipt of such a decision prefer an appeal to such officer who is senior in rank to the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer as the case may be, in each public authority. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can I seek reasons for an administrative decision that affected me?
record.expected_answer: Yes. Section 4(1)(d) requires public authorities to give reasons for administrative and quasi-judicial decisions to affected persons — and via RTI you can obtain the file notings and material behind the decision.

question: Is there a limit on how old the information I can request can be?
response: Under Section 18 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Powers and functions of Information Commissions), information older than 5 years is presumed to be correct. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Is there a limit on how old the information I can request can be?
record.expected_answer: No age limit on requests — but authorities need only provide information held or under their control; records may have been lawfully destroyed per retention schedules. question: Who is an Assistant Public Information Officer (APIO)?
response: Under Section 6 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Request for obtaining information), an Assistant Public Information Officer (State Assistant Public Information Officer) is an officer designated by the State Public Information Officer. record.question: Who is an Assistant Public Information Officer (APIO)?
record.expected_answer: APIOs (e.g. at sub-district level and designated post offices) receive RTI applications and appeals and forward them to the PIO/appellate authority — useful where the PIO sits far away. Filing via APIO adds 5 days to the response clock.

question: My RTI reply came but pages are missing and the copy is illegible. What now?
response: Under Section 7 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Time limit for providing information), the RTI reply must be provided within 30 days. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: My RTI reply came but pages are missing and the copy is illegible. What now?
record.expected_answer: File a first appeal pointing out incomplete/illegible supply — incomplete information equals deemed refusal for those parts. Ask for inspection of the original file (RTI includes the right to inspect records and take notes/certified copies on payment).

question: Can an RTI activist facing threats get protection?
response: Under Section 225 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public servant), an RTI activist can get protection. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: Can an RTI activist facing threats get protection?
record.expected_answer: Yes — report threats to police (criminal intimidation, 351 BNS); the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 exists but is largely un-operationalised, so in practice protection comes via police, human rights commissions, and CIC directions for life-liberty-related disclosures (48-hour clock).

question: Are Section 24 'excluded organisations' totally outside RTI?
response: Under Section 24 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Act not to apply to certain organisations), nothing contained in this Act shall apply to the intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule, being organisations established by the Central Government or any information furnished by such organisations to that Government. record.question: Are Section 24 'excluded organisations' totally outside RTI?
record.expected_answer: No. Intelligence and security organisations listed in the Second Schedule (IB, RAW, CBI, etc.) are excluded — except for information pertaining to allegations of corruption and human rights violations, which must be provided (human-rights ones with Commission approval within 45 days).

question: Can I withdraw or amend my RTI application after filing?

record.question: Can I withdraw or amend my RTI application after filing?
record.expected_answer: There is no statutory procedure for amendment; practically you file a fresh, better-worded application (cheap and faster than fighting over interpretation). Appeals can be withdrawn. Keep each RTI specific: one subject, numbered queries, defined period.

record.question: Whom does Section 85 BNS punish and with what?

question: Is taking or giving dowry itself an offence, even without harassment?

question: What is 'stridhan' and can I recover it after separation?

record.question: What is 'stridhan' and can I recover it after separation?
record.expected_answer: Stridhan is a woman's absolute property — gifts, jewellery, earnings received before/at/after marriage. It is distinct from dowry and from joint family property.

question: Can a wife claim maintenance while the divorce case is still pending?

question: What is the POSH Act complaint process at a workplace?
response: Under Section 9 of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (Complaint of sexual harassment), any aggrieved woman may make, in writing, a complaint of sexual harassment at workplace to the Internal Committee if so constituted, or the Local Committee, in case it is not so constituted, within a period of three months from the date of incident and in case of a series of incidents, within a period of three months from the date of last incident. This is legal information, not legal advice — consult a licensed advocate for anything consequential.

record.question: What is the POSH Act complaint process at a workplace?

question: My office has no Internal Committee though we are 30 employees. Is that punishable?

question: A cheque given to me bounced. What is the step-by-step legal process?

record.question: I missed sending the demand notice within 30 days of the return memo. Is my remedy gone?
record.expected_answer: The Section 138 cause of action for that presentation is lost — but you can re-present the cheque within its validity and send a timely notice on the fresh dishonour (successive presentations are allowed). Otherwise, pursue civil recovery of the debt.
